And those who have leafed through our books of Law with some judgment are not ignorant that the penalty of the sword may be taken in two senses, Naturally and Civilly. The natural penalty of the sword cuts and makes dissection of members <sup class="mk" data-key="n">n</sup>, and most often separation of body and soul <sup class="mk" data-key="o">o</sup>. The civil one is imposed more lightly (by reason, as I have said, of the circumstances), in banishment, and galleys for a certain time or perpetually <sup class="mk" data-key="p">p</sup>; nay, if we speak according to the constitutions of the Roman Pontiffs, in excommunication and ecclesiastical censures only <sup class="mk" data-key="q">q</sup>. And although the law of God punished both the adulterous man and the adulterous woman with death <sup class="mk" data-key="r">r</sup>, nevertheless our emperors, as to the woman, ordain otherwise: whom they have willed to be chastised, and afterwards put into a monastery, whence the husband has the faculty, within two years, of recovering her; which having passed (if the husband takes no account of her), she is bound to take the habit of that convent, to remain there and bewail her sin perpetually <sup class="mk" data-key="ſ">ſ</sup>. On the contrary, Romulus, desiring greater chastity and continence in women <sup class="mk" data-key="t">t</sup>, punished them with death, and left the men unpunished <sup class="mk" data-key="u">u</sup>. Whence afterwards was drawn the usage that the husband might kill with impunity his wife found in adultery, and nevertheless the wife dared not so much as touch with the tip of her finger the husband caught in a like fault — which did not contain in itself (said Cato holily) right, reason, nor rectitude of justice <sup class="mk" data-key="x">x</sup>. But what! if we wished to punish adulterers according to the manners or laws of the Gentiles, certainly we should find ourselves greatly confused: for some have chastised them in one way, others in another: some punished severely, as the Parthians, Egyptians, Locrians and Arabs; others gently, as the Lepreans, Gortynians and Pisidians; and some have left this crime wholly unpunished, as the Indians, Massagetae and certain other nations, among whom one may well place the Nomads, who have always wished to have their wives in common among them <sup class="mk" data-key="y">y</sup>. notes.gloss: The penalty of the Cornelian law is deportation to an island and loss of all goods, but today the humbler are put to death and the better-born deported.

notes.citation: Novels, Ut nulli iudicum (Nov. 134), chapter 10, § Si dixero (ninth collatio); the authentica Sed hodie inserted in Code 9.9 (Ad legem Iuliam de adulteriis)
notes.original: p. ſi dixero. vt nulli iud. colla. ix. aux nou uelles aut. ſed hodie. C. de adult.
notes.gloss: Nov. 134.10: the adulteress is whipped and shut in a monastery; her husband may take her back within two years, failing which she takes the habit for life.

notes.citation: Digest 23.2 (De ritu nuptiarum), l. Palam, § Quae in adulterio (D. 23.2.43.12, Ulpian); Code 6.57 (Ad senatus consultum Orfitianum), the penultimate law
notes.original: l. Palam. P. que in adulte rio. D. de rit. nup. l. penul. C. ad Orficia
notes.gloss: D. 23.2.43.12: a woman taken in adultery is as one condemned in a public trial, and may not marry a senator.

notes.original: Plutarque en la vie de Romule.
notes.gloss: Romulus's law on divorce, which allowed a husband to put away his wife for adultery and punished the wife only.

notes.original: Aule Gelle au liure x. c. xxiij.
notes.gloss: Cato's speech: a husband who catches his wife in adultery may kill her without trial, but she dare not touch him with a finger if she catches him — "nor is it right that she should", says Cato, whom Coras reads as condemning the inequality.

notes.citation: Strabo, Geography, book 16 (16.4.25, the Arabs who hold their wives in common); Alexander ab Alexandro (Alexandre Neapolitain), Genialium dierum libri, book 4, chapter 1
notes.original: Strabon au liure xvj. de la Geographie. Alexandre Neapolitein au iiij. de ſes iours Geniaux c. i.
notes.gloss: Alexander's chapter surveys the marriage customs and adultery laws of the nations Coras lists.
